notes.meaning: Solomon made up his mind to build two things. First came a temple for "the Name of the LORD," which means for God himself. Then came a palace for himself as king. Matthew Henry notes that God's house came first, because God should be served first. In this book the temple is the main story, and the palace is only mentioned in passing.

Solomon counted out a huge work force. Some carried loads, some cut stone in the hills, and some were bosses over the rest. First Kings gives 3,300 bosses, not 3,600. The Geneva notes and Keil & Delitzsch explain the gap this way: Chronicles counts every kind of overseer, high and low, while Kings counts only one group.

Solomon wrote to Hiram, king of the seaport city of Tyre. Huram and Hiram are the same name, spelled two ways. Solomon reminds him of his old friendship with David, who got cedar wood from Hiram to build his house. Matthew Henry says we may look for kindness from our parents' friends and should keep those friendships going.

Solomon explains what the temple is for. It is a place to worship God. Incense would be burned there, the holy bread called the showbread would always be set out before God, and offerings would be made every day and on feast days. Matthew Henry notes that Solomon openly tells a foreign king about Israel's worship, because true faith has nothing to hide. Since this worship was to go on forever, the building had to be strong and lasting.

The temple will be great because Israel's God is greater than all other gods. Matthew Henry says no building could ever match how great God is. But the size of the temple showed how highly God's people honored him. Wesley adds that the inner temple was small, but the buildings around it were large and many.

Solomon speaks with real humility. Not even the highest heavens can hold God, so no house can hold him either. The temple is not God's home but a place where people can come and worship him. The Geneva notes add that no one can honor God as fully as he deserves.

Solomon asks for a master craftsman to lead his own skilled workers. Like Bezalel, who led the work on the tabernacle (the worship tent of Moses' time), this man had to be skilled in many kinds of work. Tyre was famous for its colored cloth and fine carving. Matthew Henry says that work for God should be the best of its kind, so Solomon wanted the best workers he could find.

Solomon also asks for wood, especially fine cedar and cypress from the mountains of Lebanon. Hiram's men were known for their skill at cutting timber, and Solomon's men would work beside them. Nobody is sure what algum wood was, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say it did not grow in Lebanon but came through Hiram. The temple was to be "great and wonderful," so no cost was spared.

Solomon promises to pay the woodcutters with large amounts of wheat, barley, wine, and olive oil. A cor was a large measure, roughly 394 liters. Matthew Henry says employers should see that workers are well paid and well fed. First Kings mentions a different yearly payment. Older writers explain that the Kings payment went to Hiram's court, while this one fed the workmen.

Hiram wrote back with a warm letter. He says God made Solomon king because God loves his people. Matthew Henry points out that it says God loves the people, not just Solomon. A wise and good ruler is a gift from God to a nation, and kings should rule for the good of their people.

Hiram praises the LORD, the God of Israel, as the maker of heaven and earth. He thanks God for giving David such a wise son to build the temple. Matthew Henry and Wesley thought Hiram may have come to worship Israel's God. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown are more careful and say we cannot be sure.

Hiram sends a gifted craftsman named Huram-abi. The "abi" part means "my father." Keil & Delitzsch take it as a title of honor, something like "master" or "adviser." It does not mean the man was the king's own father.

This craftsman had an Israelite mother and a father from Tyre. He could work with metals, stone, wood, cloth, and every kind of carving, much like Bezalel of old. First Kings says his mother was from the tribe of Naphtali. Older writers explain this in different ways, such as family ties to both tribes or a Danite woman living in Naphtali. Matthew Henry and Wesley see his mixed family as a picture of Jews and Gentiles (non-Jews) one day joined together in the gospel.

Hiram accepts Solomon's offer and asks him to send the promised food for the workers. It was a fair business deal, not a favor or a handout. Matthew Henry notes that Hiram counted on Solomon to keep his word.
Hiram promises all the wood Solomon needs. His men would tie the logs into rafts and float them down the coast to the port of Joppa. From there Solomon's men would carry them up to Jerusalem.

Solomon counted all the foreigners living in Israel, as David had done before him. Keil & Delitzsch say these were mostly descendants of the Canaanites who had stayed in the land. Wesley says Solomon counted again because many may have died since David's count. Some older writers add that this count was not done out of pride, unlike David's sinful census.

Solomon put these foreign workers to work carrying loads, cutting stone, and overseeing. Matthew Henry and Wesley say he did not use free-born Israelites for this hard labor. Henry adds that the workers were surely paid, since God's law forbade mistreating foreigners. Having so many workers helped the great temple get finished in just seven years.
